transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jamal (Redwood SRE), Lina (Redwood SE), Sara (Nimbus Head of ML), Marcus (Nimbus Platform), Olivia (Nimbus SRE), David (Nimbus Security)

Summary (auto): Discussed design patterns for instrumenting Redwood inference with OpenTelemetry, token-level metrics, export pipelines to OTLP collector, and dashboarding. Action items and pilot plan agreed.

00:00 Alex: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off, this is Alex from Redwood, with Priya and Jamal, uh we wanted to run a deep dive on observability and specifically OpenTelemetry and token-level metrics, is that still the right agenda?
00:08 Sara: yes thanks Alex, that's right. We're particularly interested in token latency per request and correlating that with KV cache hits and batching so we can understand tail latencies.
00:18 Priya: perfect, we'll walk through two pieces: trace/span model for generation (where to put spans for request, model forward, KV cache lookup, decode) and metrics (histograms for token latency, counters for kv_cache_hit/miss, batch sizes). We'll also show example OTLP configs and Grafana dashboards.
00:33 Marcus: quick note, we run everything in a VPC and often on-prem clusters for regulated flows; need to be sure any OTEL exporters can point to our self-hosted collector and not phone home.
00:43 Jamal: yep totally, Redwood supports OTLP over gRPC/HTTP to a collector you own; there's an example collector config we'll share. For private/on-prem deployments we recommend using local collector and a sidecar or daemonset pattern.
01:02 Olivia: are there any PII concerns with spans or token logs? We can't log full prompts for compliance.
01:08 Priya: good question; we provide redaction hooks and you can choose to emit only token latency and token counts, not token text. The span attributes can include hashed prompt IDs, model_version, route, but not raw prompt.
01:22 Sara: ok show me the span layout.
01:28 Priya: demo slide - imagine a root span: /generate request, then child spans: preproc, routing, model_infer, kv_cache_lookup, decode/stream. model_infer itself can have subspans for attention kernel/quant steps if you want that granularity. We include attributes: sequence_length, batch_size, model_variant, kv_cache_hit (bool), token_index.
01:50 Marcus: token_index - that's a lot of cardinality, any guidance?
01:54 Priya: yes you don't want every token_index as a label for Prometheus; instead we recommend token_index as a span attribute only (for traces) and for metrics use aggregated histograms per route/model with bucketing for per-token latency percentiles.
02:12 Alex: think of two surface areas: traces for detailed debugging (Jaeger/Honeycomb) and metrics for SLOs/alerts (Prometheus/Grafana). Traces can be sampled (1-5%) and metrics emitted at full resolution but aggregated.
02:27 Sara: how do you export token-level histograms?
02:30 Priya: we emit a per-token-latency histogram metric, e.g., redwood.infer.token_latency_seconds bucketed; we tag by model, route, and quantization_profile. Also counters for redwood.infer.kv_cache_hit_total and _miss_total and a gauge for current_batch_size.
02:49 Olivia: does that blow up cardinality with routes? We have dozens of routes and many customers.
02:53 Priya: we recommend label cardinality limits: route (coarse), env, model; avoid adding customer-specific IDs as labels. Use attribute/span-level metadata for high-cardinality fields and sample traces for deep dives.
03:11 Marcus: what about batching - we saw throughput improves but tail latency gets worse; how do we reflect that?
03:17 Jamal: we record batch_size histogram and per-token latency histogram correlated by batch_size. In dashboards we can break token latency percentiles by batch_size buckets to see tail effects. Also we emit a metric for kv_cache_hit_ratio which is key because cache hits reduce decode cost.
03:33 Sara: can we show example dashboards?
03:36 Priya: yes, here's a sample Grafana layout I pulled together: top row SLOs (p50/p95/p99 token latency), second row KV cache metrics (hit_rate, latency), third row batching (batch size distribution, throughput vs latency), fourth row resource metrics (GPU% utilization, mem). We'll attach the dashboard JSON.
03:57 Marcus: great. For on-prem we run Prometheus + Grafana and Jaeger. Can Redwood's OTLP payload be scraped or do we need a collector?
04:05 Priya: you should run a collector; Redwood's runtime can export OTLP directly but best practice is collector as an ingest point, then route to Prometheus (via prometheus receiver) and Jaeger/Honeycomb. Collector also lets you apply sampling and redaction.
04:22 David: security question - can the OTLP connection be mutual TLS to our collector?
04:26 Jamal: yes mTLS is supported; we can provide cert config examples. For hosted Redwood we can also push metrics to your collector over VPN or private peering.
04:40 Sara: let's talk quantization signals - we think 4-bit quantized models save cost but sometimes cause token time spikes. Any metrics to watch?
04:48 Priya: we emit quantization_profile as a label and also a per-model quality regression metric (redwood.eval.quality_score) that you can bind to prompt set evals. For latency you will see higher variance on model_infer span for certain quant profiles. We recommend running A/B with tracing enabled at low sample rates and full metrics to detect regressions.
05:10 Alex: another useful signal is partial_decode_time per token when using streaming; that shows when decode stalls mid-stream.
05:18 Olivia: what about KV cache internals - keys, TTLs, and hit semantics?
05:22 Priya: we emit kv_cache_lookup_duration_seconds, kv_cache_hit_total, kv_cache_miss_total, and kv_cache_size gauge. We do not emit raw keys. For TTLs we emit a distribution of time since insertion for evicted entries so you can watch churn.
05:38 Marcus: can we correlate a trace of a slow request to the batch and the cache behavior?
05:42 Priya: yes traces include batch_id attribute on spans and a per-request trace_id. If you capture a trace for a slow request you can see the model_infer child spans and the kv_cache_lookup child. If a batch stall happened you'll see multiple request spans chained to a single batch span.
06:00 Sara: what's the recommended sampling rate to catch intermittent tail spikes?
06:04 Jamal: we usually recommend dynamic sampling: keep 1% always, bump to 10% for error conditions or when latency anomaly detectors fire, and for canary tests you can run 100% traces for a short window. Collector-side sampling rules make this manageable.
06:20 Marcus: ok instrument-wise, do we add an SDK call in our app or rely on Redwood runtime to emit OTLP?
06:25 Priya: Redwood runtime emits those metrics and spans by default when enabled in config. If you want app-level correlation, add a small SDK snippet to propagate your request_id as traceparent so spans link. We'll provide a code sample.
06:36 Alex: demo time - Priya walks through a config file and a small Grafana screenshot.
06:40 Priya: (screen) Here's a collector YAML: otlp receiver, prometheus exporter, jaeger exporter. We set service.pipelines.traces -> otlp, metrics -> prometheus. Important flags: keep_resource_attributes = true, add_tail_sampling for traces, attr redaction processor configured to drop prompt_text.
07:05 Sara: can we see how token histograms look?
07:08 Priya: (shows) token latency histogram with exponential buckets 0.5ms to 500ms; p50/p95/p99 are labeled. You can do rate() over buckets to get per-second token throughput.
07:28 Olivia: are the histograms derived in runtime or in collector?
07:31 Priya: runtime emits proto histograms; collector can convert to prometheus-compatible metrics. We avoid sending raw per-token events to reduce bandwidth.
07:42 Marcus: how do we attach model_version and commit hash without exploding cardinality?
07:46 Priya: use model_version at a coarse grain (major.minor) and commit hash only in traces or as annotation for canaries. Don't use commit hash as a metric label.
07:59 Sara: what's the overhead of emitting these metrics/traces?
08:03 Jamal: very small on CPU, network depends on sampling. Metrics are lightweight; traces at 1% add negligible cost. We measured ~2-5% CPU overhead in a Dedicated workload when full tracing enabled. We'll share the perf numbers.
08:20 Alex: alright let's talk about diagnostic payloads - what we need from you to run a benchmark.
08:24 Marcus: we can provide a representative prompt set and QPS target; we want to test both hosted and Dedicated variants.
08:30 Alex: good - we'll provide a harness script that runs through prompts at configured QPS, captures metrics to your collector, and logs per-token latencies to a local CSV for the pilot.
08:40 Priya: the harness supports variable batch policies: max_wait_ms and max_tokens_per_batch; we'll test different configs to find the knee for your latency SLO.
08:52 Sara: any gotchas for VPC/on-prem?
08:55 Jamal: if you run Private (VPC) we recommend placing collector in same VPC; if on-prem without outbound, run collector as daemonset and write to local storage or forward to internal metrics stack. Also consider disk retention for histograms.
09:12 Marcus: what's the minimal telemetry to enable in prod for SLO alerting?
09:16 Priya: token_latency histograms, kv_cache_hit_ratio gauge, batch_size histogram, and a model_infer_error counter. Those let you alert on p99 token latency and sudden cache drop.
09:28 Sara: show me an example alert rule for p99 token latency.
09:31 Priya: prometheus rule: record: job:token_latency_p99 -> histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_infer_token_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route, model)). Alert if job:token_latency_p99 > threshold for 5m.
09:58 David: on security, we need to ensure OTel collector configs are audited; can Redwood sign off on a config review?
10:03 Alex: yes we can do a config review as part of the pilot. We'll redact any sensitive attributes and provide a hardened example.
10:12 Marcus: do you support pushing metrics into our Datadog or do we need Prom?
10:16 Priya: collector can export to Datadog, Splunk, Honeycomb, etc. We'll show exporter examples. Prometheus is common for long-term metrics.
10:28 Sara: one more on sampling: for rare failures we want traces for each failure event but not normal requests. How do we configure that?
10:34 Jamal: use tail-based sampling in collector: keep all traces where model_infer_error>0 or token_latency>some threshold. This requires collector to have enough memory for tail sampling buffer.
10:48 Priya: ok moving into examples of dashboards and the specific token-level panels we recommend: p50/p95/p99 token latency over time, stacked by model_variant; token latency heatmap by token position (first 50 tokens vs later tokens) to see prefix cache effects; batch size distribution; kv_cache hit ratio by route.
11:12 Marcus: heatmap by token position would be super useful to see when KV cache warms. How do you compute that?
11:17 Priya: we emit token_index attr to spans; collector can aggregate token_index ranges into buckets and emit a heatmap. Alternatively compute offline from raw CSVs from the harness.
11:30 Sara: ok are there any pre-made dashboards we can import?
11:33 Priya: yes we'll attach a Grafana JSON for a token-metrics dashboard and a tracing quickstart for Jaeger.
11:42 Alex: let's discuss rollouts and A/B: how do we monitor quality regressions while quantizing or changing batch policy?
11:48 Priya: tie eval alerts to real-time metrics: run a prompt set eval job and emit redwood.eval.quality_score and compare against baseline; alert if degradation > threshold. Also run canary traces at higher sampling for the variant.
12:05 Marcus: technical question: can Redwood's runtime add OpenTelemetry context headers so our services can link logs to traces?
12:10 Priya: yes we propagate W3C traceparent headers. If you pass request_id we'll put it into resource attributes.
12:20 Olivia: any recommendations for long-term retention of token histograms? They can be large.
12:24 Priya: keep metrics at high resolution short term (7-30d) for debugging and rollups for long-term (90d+). Use Prometheus remote write to a long-term store if needed.
12:35 Sara: if we run pilot on Dedicated, will we get the same telemetry?
12:39 Jamal: yes Dedicated has the same telemetry; you have full control of the collector and exporters. We can also ship a lightweight sidecar in Dedicated for local scraping.
12:52 Alex: ok I'm going to capture the agreed pilot: Redwood provides harness and dashboard JSON; Nimbus runs harness for 2 hours at target QPS with two configs (hosted comparable and Dedicated quanta) and shares results; Redwood will prepare Dedicated sizing and estimated cost.
13:10 Marcus: timeline looks good. We'll try to run the test next week.

(Transcript continues with detailed Q&A snippets and clarifications)

42:05 Priya: one detail - for KV cache we recommend emitting a TTL eviction metric and a large_key_warning gauge to detect pathological workloads that create many small prefixes.
42:20 Sara: ok, helpful.
42:28 David: on the config review, we'll need a SOC2/ISO appendix; do you have that?
42:33 Alex: yes we have SOC2 Type II docs and a compliance pack. We'll share the security pack and a mapping for auditors.
42:44 Sara: quick question - can we run a short 100% tracing window during canaries?
42:49 Jamal: yes, collector rule or runtime flag can enable full tracing for canary rollout windows.
43:05 Priya: final note: for token-level SLOs we sometimes compute p99 token latency only on first N tokens to avoid skew from very long tails due to long generations; decide what maps to your UX.
43:20 Alex: great, let's recap actions...
43:24 Alex: Priya will send OTLP collector examples, dashboard JSON, and code snippets. Marcus will run harness. Alex will prepare Dedicated sizing and a brief runbook for the pilot.
43:38 Sara: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
43:41 Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with assets and schedule the pilot review for mid-March.

End of transcript.
